title: 'Dire' future ahead amid multi-million-pound HSCP funding black hole
excerpt: West Dunbartonshire HSCP faces a £16.5m funding gap, with council leader William Rooney warning the future looks "dire" without major…
content:
In a council meeting on September 29, Councillor Martin Rooney probed the board on the upcoming multi-million-pound funding gap for the next two financial years.

He said: "The forecast gap for 2027/28 is £12.7m, and then the cumulative effect for the subsequent year, assuming we didn’t make any savings on that, would go up to £16.5m in 28/29.

“It's really looking pretty dire for the future.”

Martin Rooney (Image: WDC)

Julie Slavin, chief financial officer of West Dunbartonshire HSCP, called the funding gap a “worst-case scenario", rather than a “likely case scenario.”

She added: “I think the position that we are in is more positive than it has been, and it’s certainly more favourable than some of the other integration joint boards (IJBs) across Scotland, but the pressure we are experiencing are common across all those integration joint boards.

"It’s a combination of demographic pressures, changes in policy that are not fully funded, and our partner organisations are also struggling to balance their pressures against the funding received.

“There is still work to do, but we will continue to do that.”

The current funding pressures on the HSCP have materialised from care at home and older people care due to "community workforce costs" such as overtime and agency, as well as "demand for community-based care."

It has been noted that both areas will remain under review.

Julie argued that West Dunbartonshire is in a comparably good position compared to other IJBs due to use of reserves and support of savings programs.

This funding shortfall comes as savings are expected to be made through pre-agreed changes to what the council is expected to pay into the Strathclyde Pension Fund.

The Committee for the pension fund agreed on September 23 that employer contributions from the council will reduce to 6.5% for 2027/28 and 2028/29, with the potential to maintain the rate if funding conditions are met.

This will not affect personal pensions, but it will instead allow for the council to make a saving in this area as they will be expected to pay less due to built-up surplus.

The figures presented by Councillor Rooney do not reflect the savings made by the pension contribution.

In the HSCP meeting, Julie explained the expected savings.

She said: “Any benefit from the reduction in employers' contribution to the 6.5% has not been fed into the system.

“Clearly the board will have a view on whether we take those benefits in full in the year in question or whether you would look to spread it out over a longer period.

“Our high-level estimates would be that our savings in reducing to 6.5% for next year would be about £3m.”

However, if £3m in savings is achieved for the next financial year, the funding black hole would still stand at £9.710m for 2027/28.

This comes as the HSCP is forecasting a £51,000 overspend in 2026/27, equivalent to 0.02% of its annual budget, after all planned transfers to and from earmarked reserves for the current financial year. However, many financial challenges loom for the years ahead.
